rationale:
Replace the plain list kept sorted with bisect.insort and del by index with a SortedList from the sortedcontainers package. Insertion, removal and indexed median lookup would then be sublinear for large windows. Keep the deque of arrival order for choosing the value to evict.
Why it should win: _running_median_windowed holds 4.4% of self time over 100k calls. Each step does an O(window) list insert and delete via memmove. For large windows a bucketed list reduces this. For small windows it may n

ot help, so the gain depends on the window size.
Precondition: The project must be allowed to add sortedcontainers as a dependency. The benchmark window size must be large (hundreds or more) for the gain to appear. Values must be orderable.
What the relaxed rule changes: The ordered multiset contents and the median indexing are the same, so yielded medians are identical. The change for users is a new runtime dependency.
title: Use sortedcontainers SortedList for windowed running median instead of list insort/del

rationale:
Change bucket value retrieval so that on the first request for any key the parent iterator is consumed eagerly in one tight loop, partitioning all items into per-key lists. Later requests then return iterators over those lists with no per-item generator frame, key call or cache check. Keys may then be discovered and items materialised in a different order than lazy consumption.
Why it should win: _get_values is the top hotspot (7.7% self, 250k calls). Each item costs a generator resume, a next()

call, a key call, a comparison and a cache lookup. Draining once by key removes the repeated cache scanning and per-item generator overhead.
Precondition: The relaxed rule must allow the interleaving of side effects, and the order in which items are pulled from the parent and keys are first seen, to differ. The parent iterable must be finite, and the key and validator must be pure. Within each key, item order must stay the same.
What the relaxed rule changes: Per-key item sequences and contents

stay identical. What changes for users: the parent is consumed fully at first access instead of lazily, so infinite inputs or side-effecting iterators behave differently, and the order of any cross-key output may differ.
title: Bucket: drain parent once into per-key lists when order of emission may differ

rationale:
Replace the deque-of-(level, iterator) stack with a plain list stack. Where output order may be relaxed, flatten sibling leaf items of each node in a batch (for example by partitioning a node's children into leaves and sub-containers, emitting all leaves first and then descending into the containers). This avoids the save and restore of node_group per nested child.
Why it should win: collapse has 62k calls and 4% self time. Each nested child triggers appendleft twice, a popleft and a tuple unpac

k, and re-enters the for loop. Batching leaves reduces the per-child stack churn.
Precondition: The relaxed rule must allow the flattened output to appear with leaves of a node before leaves of its nested children. The node's children must be a finite, re-iterable sequence, or be materialised to a list.
What the relaxed rule changes: The multiset of flattened leaves is identical, but the order may differ from the left-to-right depth-first order. Users who rely on sequence order would see a chang
ed order. Lazy consumption of infinite or generator inputs is lost for the materialised children.
title: Collapse: process nested children depth-first with a single flat loop instead of a deque of iterators

rationale:
Let the package build a small compiled artefact at install time that implements the sliding-window min, max and mean kernels as C-level iterators. running_min, running_max and running_mean would use it when it is importable. Otherwise they would fall back to the current pure-Python generators unchanged.
Why it should win: The three windowed kernels each get 200002 calls and together take about 17% of self time. Each item costs deque pops, a tuple allocation and generator resume overhead, all of

which a compiled loop removes.
Precondition: The build relaxation must allow a compiled extension to be produced at install time. The pure-Python fallback must remain for installs without a compiler. The extension must compare values with the same Python rich-comparison semantics (the not-less-than and not-greater-than forms) so that ties and mixed numeric types behave identically.
What the relaxed rule changes: Yielded values are identical, because the same comparison operators are used and the
same elements are returned. For users, the install now optionally compiles code. Behaviour on platforms without the extension is unchanged.
title: Install-time compiled (C-extension) versions of the windowed running min/max/mean kernels

rationale:
Ship an optional compiled helper built at install time that implements collapse's depth-first traversal with an explicit stack in C. It would special-case str, bytes and base_type, and would keep the levels semantics. collapse would delegate to it when available and otherwise use the existing generator.
Why it should win: collapse has about 62501 calls and 3.9% self time. Each node pays isinstance checks, iter() and stack manipulation in the interpreter, which a compiled loop makes cheaper.
Prec

ondition: The build relaxation must allow an optional compiled extension. The helper must preserve lazy evaluation, the exact levels cutoff, and the TypeError-based leaf detection from iter().
What the relaxed rule changes: The same sequence of leaves is yielded in the same order, and laziness is preserved. Users see only an optional compile step at install time.
title: Install-time generated, compiled collapse flattening for common nested list/tuple shapes

rationale:
Change the internal contract of the windowed min helper so the monotonic queue stores bare values in one deque and the matching indices in a second one. The expiry check then compares the front of the index deque only. Apply the same layout to the max helper. Callers are unchanged, but the helper's private state layout and the cost per item change.
Why it should win: The helper runs 200k calls with 0.18s self time. Each item builds an (index, value) tuple and does repeated sis[0][0] and sis[-1][

1] double indexing.
Precondition: Private helpers are only called from running_min and running_max; values are mutually comparable with < exactly as now.
What the relaxed rule changes: The same comparisons are made in the same order, so the yielded minima are identical. Only the private storage layout changes; users see no difference.

label: relax_api

rationale:
Add a build or install step that generates a flattened module variant of SortedList.add. The variant contains the fast path of _expand (index increment loop, load-based split check) inline and uses a precomputed double-load constant. The package loads the generated variant at import and falls back to the hand-written add if it is missing.
Why it should win: SortedList.add is called 292k times and _expand 292k times, together about 17% of self time. Each add pays a Python method call plus repeate

d attribute lookups. A generated specialisation removes the call and the per-call shifts.
Precondition: The install-time rule must allow a generated source file in the package, created at install and imported at runtime. The generator must reproduce add and _expand semantics, including subclass overrides of _expand and _load.
What the relaxed rule changes: The generated function performs the same list mutations in the same order, so the resulting container state and output digest are identical.
The only user-visible change is an extra generated file and an import-time selection.
title: Install-time generated specialised SortedList.add with the expand check inlined and bisect locals bound

rationale:
Give SortedList a new public method that takes a value plus a precomputed 'known absent' guarantee and does the append/insort and the length-bookkeeping in one frame, with the load-split check performed inline. SortedDict.__setitem__ then calls it directly instead of going through the cached add and a separate _expand call.
Why it should win: SortedDict.__setitem__ has 150k calls with 0.48s cumulative; each one runs a SortedList.add (0.70s cumulative incl. _expand). Fusing add and _expand remove

s two Python frames per insertion for the dict path.
Precondition: The public API of SortedList may gain a new method; SortedDict callers switch to it. No existing signature is removed.
What the relaxed rule changes: Resulting list contents, index and dict state are identical. Users see only one additional public method on SortedList.

label: relax_api

rationale:
Compile pyparsing/results.py with mypyc (or Cython) as an optional build-time extension, so ParseResults __new__/__init__ run as C code. Keep the pure-Python module as fallback if the extension is missing. The build tool becomes a build-time dependency only.
Why it should win: ParseResults.__new__ and __init__ together take about 9% self time over 71k calls, mostly attribute stores and isinstance checks, which compiled code speeds up considerably.
Precondition: The rule against new dependencies

must allow mypyc or Cython as a build-time tool and permit a compiled artifact in the build. The class must remain compatible with compilation: it uses dynamic attributes, a MutableMapping/MutableSequence base and a nested List class.
What the relaxed rule changes: Parse output is unchanged. For users, the package would ship platform-specific wheels with a pure-Python fallback, and tracebacks and introspection of ParseResults would differ slightly.
title: Compile hot ParseResults construction path with Cython/mypyc extension for results.py

rationale:
Build core.py as an optional compiled extension so the dispatch loop in _parseNoCache, preParse's whitespace skipping, and the And/MatchFirst/Forward parseImpl methods avoid interpreter overhead. Retain the pure-Python source as a fallback.
Why it should win: _parseNoCache (21.6% self time, 138k calls) and preParse (4%, 107k calls) plus the parseImpl methods account for more than half of runtime, and that is pure interpreter dispatch overhead.
Precondition: A compiler dependency (Cython or mypyc

) and a compiled artifact must be allowed. The heavy use of dynamic method rebinding (self.parseImpl = ...) and operator overloading must survive compilation.
What the relaxed rule changes: Parsing results are identical. Users would get a compiled wheel, a more complex build, and different stack frames in tracebacks, which affects ParseException.explain.
title: Compile core.py parse engine (_parseNoCache, preParse, parseImpl) with mypyc/Cython

rationale:
At build or streamline time, compute for each element a flag saying whether preParse is a no-op (no ignoreExprs and no skipWhitespace). Also precompute a regex-based skipper from whiteChars (a compiled pattern for the whitespace run). In _parseNoCache, skip the preParse call when the flag says it is a no-op, and use the compiled pattern's match end otherwise.
Why it should win: preParse is called 107k times with 4% self time, plus call overhead inside _parseNoCache (22% self). Many elements, suc

h as Forward, And and MatchFirst, call it with callPreParse set even though they have no whitespace work to do. A precomputed flag removes the call and the per-character Python loop.
Precondition: whiteChars, skipWhitespace and ignoreExprs must not change after streamline; any setter must invalidate the cached flag and the compiled skipper. Subclasses overriding preParse must be excluded from the fast path.
What the relaxed rule changes: The same locations are returned, since a regex whitespace
run matches the same characters as the loop. The only difference is that precomputed state is built once per grammar, so outputs are byte-identical.
title: Precompute per-element whitespace-skip and fast-path flags at streamline time to drop preParse call overhead

rationale:
During streamline, compute for each MatchFirst alternative the set of possible first characters, or mark it unknown when it is not computable (Regex, Forward and so on). Build a dict from character to the ordered list of candidate alternatives. At parse time, after whitespace skipping, look up instring[loc] and try only those candidates in their original order.
Why it should win: MatchFirst.parseImpl has 27k calls and 0.88 s cumulative time. It tries alternatives that fail and raise, which is th

e source of 57k exception constructions and many _parseNoCache calls. A table avoids the doomed attempts.
Precondition: Each element's first-character set must be a sound over-approximation (Literal, Keyword, Word init chars). Anything unknown, including elements with ignoreExprs or parse actions that can match empty, is always a candidate.
What the relaxed rule changes: Skipped alternatives could never have matched, so the first successful alternative is the same and the results are identical.
Only the error message for total failure might differ, so the fast path should fall back to the full loop when nothing matches.
title: Compile first-character dispatch table for MatchFirst alternatives at streamline time

rationale:
Add a new internal method on ParserElement (a match-only variant of _parseNoCache) that returns just the end location and skips ParseResults construction and parse actions. Change the probe calls in _InfixNotation.parseImpl (_check_operand_follows, which parses with do_actions=False and discards the tokens) to use it. The internal call signature gains a new return type for these callers.
Why it should win: _parseNoCache builds a ParseResults on every successful match (71k constructions, about 9%

self time in __new__ and __init__). _check_operand_follows discards the tokens, so building them is wasted work.
Precondition: Only applies to callers that ignore tokens. Sub-expressions are still run through their own _parse, so a match-only mode must be propagated through And/MatchFirst/Forward parseImpl, or it only saves the outermost result. Parse actions with callDuringTry=True must still run.
What the relaxed rule changes: The parse outcome (success or failure and end loc) is unchanged, s
o the output is the same. Internal method signatures change; only subclass authors overriding parseImpl would be affected if the mode is propagated.
title: Add a no-results fast-path parse entry point that returns only end loc for lookahead and operand checks

rationale:
The operator stack currently stores a dict with string keys for each operator and compares enum types by lookup. Replace the dicts with a small __slots__ class or list records, and update _apply_operator and reduce_operators to read attributes. _apply_operator is a private helper, so its parameter type changes.
Why it should win: parseImpl in helpers.py has 8% self time; each operator allocates a 6-key dict and each reduction does repeated string-key lookups and tuple-in membership tests.
Precon

dition: All readers of the operator_stack dict entries (reduce_operators, _apply_operator, ternary handling) are updated together.
What the relaxed rule changes: Only the internal representation changes. The parse results are identical. No public API is affected, but private helper signatures change.

rationale:
Add mypy/mypyc as a build dependency and compile the parser and regex modules into native extension modules, keeping the annotated source as is. The Python fallback stays for environments where the extension is not built.
Why it should win: Run time is dominated by per-character Python loops and call-heavy small functions (skip_chars 502k calls, parse_value 109k calls). The code is already annotated for mypyc, which gives typed locals and direct calls and removes interpreter overhead; mypyc-comp

iled tomli is typically 2-4x faster.
Precondition: The dependency rule must allow mypy/mypyc as a build-time dependency, and the benchmark must run against the built extension (build step before the run). The source must type-check under mypyc.
What the relaxed rule changes: Parsing semantics are unchanged because mypyc compiles the same source. Exceptions and results are identical. For users the package becomes a platform-specific binary wheel, with the pure-Python fallback kept.
title: Compile tomli's _parser.py and _re.py with mypyc as a build-time dependency

rationale:
In key_value_rule, skip the flags.is_(abs_key_parent, FROZEN) lookup when the current table (header) is known to contain no frozen ancestors, caching a per-header 'frozen-free' marker in Output that is reset whenever a table header changes. Frozen state can only change on header statements or after inserting inline values, so keep the marker updated there. Output key order of the result dict is allowed to differ, so the nest lookup can be reordered.
Why it should win: key_value_rule runs 51200 t

imes with ~9.7% self time and 80% cumulative; each call does a Flags.is_ walk over the key parent path. A cached verdict per header avoids repeated walks.
Precondition: Frozen flags of a header's ancestors do not change between statements of the same table section except through the pair's own value insertion; the relaxed rule permits dict key order in the result to differ.
What the relaxed rule changes: Same errors raised and same contents; only the insertion order of keys in result dicts might
differ, which the lens allows.
title: Defer table-flag bookkeeping for plain dotted-key-free pairs by batching pending flags

rationale:
Build once at import a table mapping each possible first character to a small handler code (basic string, literal string, true, false, array, inline table, digit or sign start, other). parse_value does one lookup and jumps to the matching branch, so numbers and dates no longer pass through the chain of string comparisons. The table could also be generated at install or build time and shipped as a module constant.
Why it should win: parse_value is called 108800 times and is the top self-time hots

pot at 9.7%. Most values are numbers, dates or strings, and each one runs several sequential char comparisons and startswith calls before reaching the regexes.
Precondition: The relaxed rule must allow import-time or install-time generated tables. The fallthrough order for all characters not specially handled must stay identical, including special floats and the error case.
What the relaxed rule changes: Same branch is chosen for each first character as in the current if-chain, including fall-th
rough from 't' and 'f' to the regexes. Output and error messages are unchanged. Users see nothing different.
title: Precompute 256-entry first-character dispatch table for parse_value at import time

rationale:
Add a per-loads memo (or a process-wide bounded cache) keyed by the source text of a bare-key segment starting at a position. A single compiled regex match for a whole bare key (parts joined by dots, with optional whitespace) returns the key tuple directly, with interned strings. Fall back to the current path for quoted keys or any mismatch.
Why it should win: parse_key runs 67200 times and parse_key_part 70400 times, with many skip_chars calls each. A 400-table document repeats the same few key

names over and over, so a single regex match plus a cache of tuples removes most per-character work.
Precondition: The regex must be compiled once at import (an artefact allowed to be generated at build time) and must accept exactly the bare-key grammar, with trailing whitespace handling identical to skip_chars. The MAX_KEY_PARTS check must still apply.
What the relaxed rule changes: Returned positions and key tuples are equal to those the current code produces. Only the string object identity
of key parts may differ, and the JSON output is the same.
title: Cache parsed key tuples and parts for repeated key text across tables

rationale:
Change the internal signatures of parse_value, parse_key_value_pair, parse_array and parse_inline_table to take a single parser-state object (holding src, parse_float and nest level) instead of four separate arguments. Callers inside the module adapt. Also resolve the nest_lvl > MAX_INLINE_NESTING check only in the array and inline-table entry points instead of on every scalar value.
